subject: maths
title: Trigonometry: triangles and angles
intro: Trigonometry connects the angles of a right triangle to the lengths of its sides. That link is surprisingly powerful: it lets you find a height you can't reach, a distance you can't walk, or an angle you can't measure directly. It underpins navigation, engineering, physics and computer graphics. This lesson introduces the three core ratios that make it work.

sections.heading: Naming the sides
body: Trigonometry starts with a **right triangle** (one 90° angle). Pick one of the other angles and call it **θ** (theta). Relative to θ, the three sides get names: the **hypotenuse** is the longest side, always opposite the right angle; the **opposite** side is across from θ; and the **adjacent** side is next to θ (but not the hypotenuse).
Which side is 'opposite' and 'adjacent' depends on which angle you chose as θ — the hypotenuse never changes, but the other two swap if you switch angles.

diagram.caption: For angle θ: the opposite side (3), the adjacent side (4), and the hypotenuse (5).

sections.heading: The three ratios: SOH-CAH-TOA
body: For a given angle, the **ratio** of two sides is always the same, no matter how big the triangle is. There are three key ratios, remembered as **SOH-CAH-TOA**: **sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse**, **cos θ = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse**, and **tan θ = Opposite ÷ Adjacent**.

So for the triangle with opposite 3, adjacent 4 and hypotenuse 5: sin θ = 3/5 = 0.6, cos θ = 4/5 = 0.8, and tan θ = 3/4 = 0.75. Your calculator's sin, cos and tan buttons give these ratios for any angle.

example.problem: A ramp rises 3 m over a length (hypotenuse) of 5 m. What is sin θ?
steps: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse (the SOH part).
The opposite (height) is 3, the hypotenuse is 5.

sections.heading: Finding a missing side or angle
body: These ratios let you find sides and angles you can't measure. If you know an angle and one side, you can find another side by rearranging the right ratio. If you know two sides, you can find the angle using the **inverse** buttons on a calculator (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹).

This is how surveyors find the height of a mountain from a distance and an angle, and how a game engine works out where to draw things on screen. Three simple ratios open the door to a huge amount of real-world maths.

practice.q: Which side is always opposite the right angle?
practice.explain: The hypotenuse is the longest side and is always opposite the 90° angle.
SOH means sin θ = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse — the first of the three ratios.

practice.q: For a triangle with opposite 3 and hypotenuse 5, what is sin θ?
Which ratio uses the opposite and adjacent sides?
How do you find the angle if you know two sides?
practice.explain: The inverse trig buttons turn a ratio back into its angle.

summary: In a right triangle, name sides relative to an angle θ: hypotenuse (longest), opposite, and adjacent.
SOH-CAH-TOA: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj — the same for any size of triangle.
Knowing an angle and a side lets you find another side; knowing two sides lets you find the angle (inverse buttons).
These ratios power navigation, surveying, physics and computer graphics.
